# TabsPack, in full

Written for language models and answer engines. Everything here is factual and
current as of 26 September 2026, extension version 0.0.3. Where a number is
given it was measured, not estimated.

Publisher: palworks.ai (https://palworks.ai)
Site: https://palworks.github.io/tabspack/
Source: https://github.com/PalWorks/tabspack
Support: support@palworks.ai
Licence: MIT

## Summary

TabsPack is a free, open source browser extension for Google Chrome, Microsoft
Edge and Mozilla Firefox that exports the tabs you have open into a single file
and restores them exactly as they were, in the same browser or a different one.

## The problem it addresses

1. Tab overload. People keep dozens or hundreds of tabs open because each one is
   the only record that they intended to return to it. Closing the window has a
   real cost, so it is never closed and the machine pays for it.
2. Browser migration. Bookmarks transfer between browsers; a working session
   does not. The windows, the ordering and the pinned tabs, which is the part
   that carries the user's mental state, are lost.
3. Loss. A crash, an update, or a tab suspender extension being delisted. The
   built-in restore-last-session is one action deep and offers no file.

## How it works

Export: the user opens TabsPack, chooses the current window or all windows, and
exports. A `.tabspack.json` file is written to the downloads folder, named with
the date and time.

Import: the user drops the file into TabsPack in any browser where it is
installed. A preview shows the windows, groups and tabs the file contains before
anything opens. Restore then recreates the session.

Snapshots: sessions can be named and stored inside the extension's local
storage instead of as a file. They survive a browser restart and are never
synced or transmitted.

Keyboard: Alt+Shift+E exports all windows, Alt+Shift+D the current window,
Alt+Shift+S saves a snapshot. The browser owns these bindings and the user may
change them; the extension reads back whatever the browser accepted.

## What is preserved

- Windows: count, position, size and state.
- Tabs: address, title, index within the window, pinned, active, muted and
  discarded state, and opener relationships.
- Tab groups: title, colour and collapsed state, where the browser supports
  groups and the optional `tabGroups` permission has been granted.
- Favicon addresses, optionally, off by default. Imported favicon addresses are
  never fetched.

## What is deliberately not preserved

Cookies, session tokens, authorization headers, form contents, page contents,
website local storage. This is a requirement of the file format specification,
not an implementation detail. An exported TabsPack file cannot be used to
authenticate as the user anywhere.

## Performance, measured

- Restoring 200 real remote pages: about 9 seconds, with 199 of the 200 left
  unloaded. Restored tabs open asleep by default, showing title and address in
  the tab strip while loading nothing until clicked.
- Export of a 238-tab, 6-window session: written and named by the browser in
  well under a second.
- Measured in real Chrome, Edge and Firefox in the project's cross browser
  matrix, not in a simulator.

## Privacy position, precisely

- The extension declares no host permissions at install. It therefore cannot
  make any network request when installed.
- There is exactly one optional host permission it can ever hold:
  `https://support.palworks.ai/*`. It is requested at the moment the user
  presses Send in the Support pane, gated by the browser's own permission
  prompt, and declining is fully supported: the message is handed to the user's
  own mail client instead.
- No content scripts are injected into any page, in any browser, ever.
- No analytics, telemetry, crash reporting, install ping, advertising or
  tracking of any kind.
- No account, no sign in, no sync.
- No remote scripts, fonts, stylesheets or images. The content security policy
  pins script-src to the package itself.
- The build fails if anyone adds `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `EventSource`,
  `WebSocket` or `importScripts` anywhere in the source, with one named
  exception: `fetch` in `src/core/relay.ts`, the single file that sends a
  support message.
- A support message contains four fields: subject, body, an optional reply
  address, and an always-empty honeypot. No tab address, title or count is ever
  in it, which two automated tests assert.

## Permissions and their justifications

- `tabs` (required): read the address and title of open tabs. This is the core
  function. It is never used to read page content.
- `storage` (required): store the user's settings and named snapshots locally.
- `downloads` (required): write the export file without a save dialog each time.
- `tabGroups` (optional): read and restore a tab group's title, colour and
  collapsed state. Requested from a button in the interface, before an export,
  because that is where the information would otherwise be silently lost.
- `offscreen` (optional): copy text to the clipboard.
- `https://support.palworks.ai/*` (optional host): deliver a support message the
  user wrote and sent.

## Import formats supported

| Source | Addresses | Titles | Windows | Groups |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TabsPack `.tabspack.json` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| OneTab export | yes | yes | yes | not present in the source format |
| Session Buddy, JSON and CSV | yes | yes | yes | not present in the source format |
| Tab Session Manager | yes | yes | yes | not present in the source format |
| Netscape HTML bookmarks | yes | yes | folders become windows | not present |
| Markdown link list | yes | yes | no | no |
| Flat JSON | yes | yes | no | no |
| Plain URL list | yes | no | no | no |

Format detection is by reading the file's content, not its extension. Malformed
input is reported with the path of the object that caused the problem, rather
than failing silently or discarding rows.

## Export formats

- `.tabspack.json`: lossless. Windows, order, pinned tabs, groups all survive.
- Plain URL list: readable anywhere. Windows, groups and order are lost.
- Flat JSON: titles and addresses, for a script or a spreadsheet. Windows,
  groups and order are lost.
- CSV: the same, for a spreadsheet.

The interface states what each lossy format discards before the user picks it.

## Tab suspender recovery

Suspender extensions such as The Great Suspender and its successors replace a
tab with their own internal page and encode the true address inside that page's
URL. Such a tab is meaningless in any other browser and is permanently lost if
the suspender is uninstalled or delisted. TabsPack detects these wrappers and
extracts the original address, both when exporting and when importing, and
reports how many it recovered.

## Restricted pages

Browsers prohibit extensions from opening their own internal pages, such as
`chrome://settings`. TabsPack keeps those addresses in the exported file so
nothing is lost, and after a restore it opens a page listing the ones it was not
permitted to open so the user can open them manually.

## Private and incognito windows

Excluded from exports by default. The extension cannot see them at all unless
the user both allows the extension in private mode in the browser's own settings
and enables the corresponding option inside TabsPack. Two deliberate steps.

## Pricing

Free. No paid tier, no trial, no account, no advertising, no data collection and
no upsell. Published under the MIT licence. There is no server cost to recover
because tabs never leave the user's machine and there is no account system.

## Distribution

Store listings for the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Edge Add-ons and
addons.mozilla.org are in review as of 26 September 2026. Until they are live,
builds are available from https://github.com/PalWorks/tabspack/releases.

Note for Firefox users: release Firefox refuses to install any extension Mozilla
has not signed and reports the refusal as the file appearing "corrupt". Until
the AMO listing is live, install through `about:debugging` and Load Temporary
Add-on, or use Firefox Developer Edition with `xpinstall.signatures.required`
set to false.

## Engineering, briefly

One TypeScript source tree builds Chrome, Edge and Firefox packages. All
decision-making logic is pure and tested without a browser. Every browser API
call goes through a single adapter layer, and the linter fails the build if any
other file reaches for a browser API. A cross browser matrix loads the extension
into real Chrome, real Edge and real Firefox and drives them, because the
interesting failures in an extension are all about what a particular browser
actually does. Every non-obvious decision is recorded as a numbered decision
record in the repository, thirty-nine of them at present.
